newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - S.Africa Dec reserves to fall, Nov PPI up.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - S.Africa Dec reserves to fall, Nov PPI up.

text.p: Reserve Bank intervention in the South African currency market and the repayment of foreign debt are expected to have brought a two-month recovery in reserves to an end in December, economists said on Friday.
A Reuters consensus poll of seven economists forecast reserves would decline to 10.85 billion rand after rising to 10.93 billion rand in November from October's rise to 10.28 billion rand.
The average forecast was drawn from a range of 10.4 to 11.2 billion rand.
Economists said the Reserve Bank was likely to have drawn down on its reserves in defence of the rand which sank to 4.75 against the dollar early last month.
Local banks were also likely to have repaid some of their offshore borrowings during December, resulting in an outflow of capital, some economists said.
"I think the Reserve Bank was in the market to protect the rand and I think there was some repayment of foreign loans by local banks so I expect a slowdown," Equisec economist Dawie Roodt said.
Econometrix chief economist Azar Jammine said he expected the repayment of debt to have been offset by capital inflows into the equity and bond markets.

Johannesburg Stock Exchange statistics show foreigners were net buyers of 505 million rand's worth of equities in December, while Bond Exchange data shows foreigners were net buyers of 959 million rand's worth of gilts during the month.

Nedcor chief economist Dennis Dykes noted that the high money market shortage indicated that there was some pressure on the balance of payments in the month and with all other factors being relatively benign, a slight drop could be expected.

The money market shortage touched a record high of 11.126 billion rand late in December -- traditionally a tight period for banks primarily because notes and coins in circulation balloon during the Christmas spending period.
However, Johan Rossouw, economist at stockbroker Huysamer Stals, said he expected the liquidity squeeze on the money market to have prompted local banks to have borrowed offshore in the month.
"I suspect reserves will have increased...because I believe that some of the banks borrowed overseas during December to avert pressure from the money market," Rossouw said.
The data will be released at 1600 GMT next Wednesday.

Also due for release next week is November producer inflation data which economists expect to show an 8.7 percent year-on-year increase and a 0.7 percent month-on-month rise from 8.3 and 1.3 percent in October.

Economists said the steep 3.0 percent month-on-month rise in the imported component in October -- largely due to higher fuel prices -- was not expected to be repeated and was likely to come in at between 0.5 and 1.0 percent on month.
The domestic component was expected to remain relatively flat, with food prices in particular showing little change as already indicated in the consumer price index for November.
The November producer price index will be released at 0900 GMT on Tuesday.
